summary: Learners read a picture of a shape and its image on a squared/coordinate grid and say precisely WHICH transformation maps one onto the other, then work the other way — producing the image from a stated transformation. The defining evidence differs per transformation: reflection reverses 'sense' (handedness) and is built with a mirror line that is the perpendicular bisector of segments joining object and image points; translation keeps orientation and sense and is described by a vector/displacement applied to every vertex; rotation keeps sense but changes orientation and must be described by three things — centre, size (angle) of turn, and direction (clockwise/anticlockwise). Fluency means translating freely between the drawn image and its precise verbal description while checking congruence throughout, including non-standard cases such as sloping mirror lines and ambiguous turn directions.
misconceptions: Calling a rotation a reflection (or vice versa) because sense/handedness is not checked.
Describing a rotation incompletely — giving the angle but omitting the centre and/or the direction.
When reflecting in a sloping mirror, keeping the image in the same horizontal/vertical plane instead of moving each point perpendicular to the mirror.
Reversing coordinates (up before across) when labelling where the image landed.

activities.title: Name it: reconstruct the transformation that produced the image
steps: On a grid showing a shape and its image already placed (produced by a rotation), work out which single transformation maps the first onto the second and reproduce it by setting the parameters yourself.
First try a reflection: flip the shape and compare handedness to the target — notice the 'sense' no longer matches (the target reads the same way round), so it cannot be a reflection.
Switch to rotation: choose a centre of rotation, set the angle of turn, and choose the direction (clockwise/anticlockwise) until your image lands exactly on the target.

State the full description aloud or in writing, e.g. 'rotation, 90° clockwise, about (2,1)', and check what each part controls: turning the same amount about a different centre makes the shape land somewhere else, and for a 90° turn, going the opposite direction lands it in a different place. (For a 180° turn, clockwise and anticlockwise give the same image, but still state the direction to keep the description complete.)
Confirm the image is congruent to the original (e.g. by tracing or matching vertices).
activities.insight: Checking sense is what distinguishes a rotation from a reflection, and a rotation is only fully specified by centre, size AND direction together. The centre and the angle always affect where the image lands. The direction matters for 90° turns, but a 180° turn lands in the same place either way.

activities.title: Produce a reflection in a sloping mirror line
steps: Given a shape and a mirror line (including sloping or offset lines, not just horizontal/vertical), draw the reflected image.
For each vertex, draw the perpendicular from the vertex to the mirror line and step an equal distance beyond it to place the image vertex.
Check that the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of each segment joining a vertex to its image, and that the sense (handedness) of the shape is reversed.
Describe what you did as 'a reflection in [this] mirror line' and confirm the image is congruent to the original.
Repeat with a sloping mirror to make sure your method does not rely on 'straight across/down'.
activities.insight: A reflection moves every point perpendicular to the mirror by an equal distance on the other side, so the mirror is the perpendicular bisector of each joining segment — this holds for sloping mirrors, not just level ones.

activities.title: Translate by a vector and label coordinates carefully
steps: Translate a shape by a given displacement (e.g. 3 right and 2 up), applying the same movement to every vertex.
Describe the movement both as a vector and in left/right/up/down words.
Label the coordinates of the translated vertices, writing each as (across, up).
Check that orientation and sense are unchanged and that the image is congruent to the original.
activities.insight: A translation slides every point by the same displacement, preserving orientation, sense and size; coordinates are read across first, then up.

activities.title: Precision check: discrete items for describing transformations
steps: Answer 'which transformation maps A to B?' where one distractor shows the same shape reflected (sense reversed) rather than rotated.
Match written descriptions to images.
Fill in the three parts of a rotation description (centre, size, direction) for a shown image.
Draw the path/image to produce a reflection in a given mirror line.
activities.insight: Describing a transformation precisely means using the correct defining marks — and a rotation description counts only when centre, angle and direction are all given.

activities.title: Annotated worked examples as a reference
steps: Study one worked example of each transformation with its defining marks revealed: the mirror line and perpendicular joining lines for reflection; the vector arrow for translation; the centre, angle arc and direction arrow for rotation.
For each, identify whether the sense is reversed and use that to decide 'rotation or reflection?'.
Use these as a reference while attempting your own naming and producing tasks.
activities.insight: Each transformation has a distinct set of marks to read; sense reversal is the tell for reflection.

checkQuestion: Show a squared grid with a scalene shape and its image, where the image is the shape turned a quarter-turn about a marked point (sense unchanged). Say: 'What single transformation maps the first shape onto the second? Describe it as fully as you can.' Then give a fresh copy of the original next to a mirror line and say: 'Now YOU produce the reflection of this shape in this mirror line, and describe what you did.' Read what they say about the shown transformation, then watch what they draw.
checkAnswer: For the shown image: 'a rotation' named with all three descriptors — centre (the marked point), size (90°/quarter turn) and direction (clockwise or anticlockwise, matching the picture) — justified by the shape keeping its sense while changing orientation. For the produced reflection: each vertex placed perpendicular to and equidistant from the mirror, sense reversed, described as a reflection in that mirror line, and the image confirmed congruent to the original.
